title: Insurance assessment for shopping centres in Moldova
excerpt: Prepare buildings, tenants, stock, shared areas, incidents and business-interruption information for shopping-centre insurance assessment.

author: ING Broker editorial team

seo.title: Shopping centre insurance assessment in Moldova | ING Broker
seo.description: Distinguish the landlord's building, tenants' stock, shared installations, visitor liability and interrupted trading when assessing shopping-centre insurance.
seo.keywords: shopping centre insurance Moldova, tenant property, shop inventory, visitor liability, rental income loss

content:
Shopping-centre insurance requires identifying each party's property and interests: owner, manager, traders and service providers. The building, shop stock and visitor liability are distinct subjects. A property policy must not be presented as automatically protecting every business in the building.

For a shopping centre in the Republic of Moldova, a well-organised file describes the actual use of premises, shared installations and dependencies between tenants. The lists in this article help prepare discussion. They do not confirm that every risk is insurable or that a provider will accept every expense category.

Map the interests within the building

Begin with the entities involved and their documented responsibilities. The owner may own the building, the manager may coordinate operations, and each trader may own its furnishings and goods. Record warehouses, food areas and spaces used temporarily for events or stands separately. Their actual use should remain visible in the assessment file.

Do not assume a single contract removes the need for clarification. Ask for identification of the property, persons and interests actually included in the proposal. If a lease requires particular insurance, have its wording checked by a competent person. A landlord's commercial requirement does not replace the conditions of an insurance contract.

Separate construction from shared installations

Prepare information about floor area, levels, materials, roof and known alterations. For installations, describe electrical supply, heating, ventilation and water networks. A technical unit may serve several shops. Local damage can stop a larger area than the room where it occurs, so explain those dependencies rather than listing only the unit's physical location.

Include existing lifts, escalators and other equipment in the appropriate inventory without stating automatic acceptance. Record who maintains them and where maintenance records are kept. A maintenance agreement is not an insurance policy and does not alone establish payment after an incident. Keep the maintenance documents distinct from the proposed insurance conditions.

What is held in shops and warehouses?

Each trader should be able to describe goods by category, value and storage location. Jewellery, electronics, clothing and food raise different questions. Avoid one total value that conceals concentration in a warehouse or display. The description should make clear which goods are held where, rather than simply reporting the centre's combined stock value.

Check goods that do not belong to the trader, such as items received for sale or repair. Present relevant documents and request clarification of the insurable interest. A supplier's goods are not automatically included merely because they are physically in the centre when an incident occurs. Ownership and the relevant contractual interest need separate identification.

Seasonality changes exposed values

Stocks can increase before holidays, during sales or when larger deliveries arrive. Prepare documented values for ordinary periods and foreseeable peaks. Do not confuse the annual average with the maximum held simultaneously in one space. A general yearly figure should not hide a concentration that exists during a particular trading period.

When comparing proposals, ask how an inventory change or new stand should be communicated. Do not assume an old policy value adjusts automatically for the season. Apply the same check to improvements made by tenants between renewals and to temporary storage outside the main building. Clarify changes against the actual proposal or contract.

Food areas deserve a separate sheet

A kitchen, oven or extraction system is used differently from a clothing shop. Describe the equipment, hours and actual activities in each area. Organise available maintenance information and do not omit an activity merely because it occupies little space. The risk description should reflect operations rather than only the amount of floor area used.

For food, separate physical refrigerator damage from spoiled products and possible consumer claims. These are different situations to check under relevant conditions. This article does not state that building insurance includes them all and does not replace food-safety rules applicable to the operator. Keep the physical asset, stock and liability questions distinct.

Shared spaces and visitors

Entrances, corridors, stairs, parking areas and delivery ramps are used by people with different interests. Record operational responsibility for cleaning, snow clearance, signs and interventions. Keep evidence of checks actually performed. Do not present this article as an exhaustive list of legal duties for managing a centre or as proof those duties have been fulfilled.

A visitor making a claim is not asking for repair of the owner's property. General liability needs assessment separately from owned assets. Ask about declared activities, included parties and defence costs if provided in the proposal. Do not infer legal liability solely from where the incident occurred; the relevant circumstances and documents still require review.

Tenant works can affect neighbours

A shop fit-out may involve interventions in installations or work presenting a fire risk. Record the periods, separated areas and companies carrying out the work. Internal notification to the centre manager does not automatically establish that a new risk is accepted under existing insurance. Keep the actual works and the proposed conditions clearly identified.

Before work starts, request assessment of conditions for existing property, the works themselves and potential third-party damage. Do not treat the contractor's agreement as a universal substitute for the owner's assessment. Photographs and an initial-condition inventory can support documentation, but do not independently decide whether a loss is covered under the relevant policy.

Rent and shop sales are different interests

When an area cannot be used, the owner and traders may experience different economic losses. The owner may have questions about rent, while traders have questions about their operations. Prepare financial documents for each entity. Do not combine revenues belonging to different companies into one value merely because they arise in the same building.

Any business-interruption component must be discussed against its own events, periods and calculation rules. Not every decline in sales is an insured event. Lack of customers, a commercial change and closure after material damage are not identical situations. Their causes and financial effects should remain distinct in both planning records and insurance questions.

Compare deductibles and limits by category

The insurance premium is the amount paid for the contract. The deductible is the portion of a loss borne by the insured under its conditions. Ask for an explanation of each rule relevant to the centre's important risks, including whether certain property categories have different thresholds or calculation formulas.

An overall sum does not alone explain limits for stock, glazing, installations or reinstatement expenses. Read exclusions as well: these are situations in which the contract does not provide cover. For a useful comparison, retain the same description of the centre and the same values in every request sent to providers.

Prepare incident procedures in advance

Assign the people who coordinate safety, tenant contact and contractual notification. Protecting people comes first after an incident. Document the situation safely and retain relevant information without publicly sharing images of affected individuals or commercial data that is unnecessary. Organising the file must not take priority over urgent measures to protect people.

Separate urgent work from measures that can await instructions. Follow policy conditions and clarify evidence retention. This article establishes neither a universal notification deadline nor acceptance of every intervention invoice.

Illustration: water affects a corridor and shops

In a hypothetical incident, damage affects a corridor and two shops. Management documents the shared installation, the owner inventories its finishes, and traders distinguish their damaged stock. Each checks the documents applicable to its own interest rather than assuming one policy pays all losses. The example describes separate records, not a single combined claim entitlement.

This is not a real case and establishes no party's fault. It explains separate records and coordinated communication. The insurer decides under documented circumstances and contract; the broker explains but does not replace that decision.

Deliveries and goods temporarily outside the shop

Goods may pass through a ramp, service corridor and receiving area. Describe this path and when the trader takes possession. A policy address alone does not explain protection's start or end at every stage.

For transport from warehouse to centre, distinguish building property insurance from CARGO. Check loading, unloading and temporary holding separately. One product name does not establish the other's conditions.

Records that can be kept current

Use a sheet for each space showing the user, activity, owned property, shared installations and recent changes. There is no need to collect personal information about every shop employee for the initial assessment. What matters initially is the risk description and appropriately designated contact people who can clarify the information.

When tenants change, check new equipment, stock and works. Replacing clothing retail with food service is more than a name on a door. Ask before assuming old conditions remain suitable.

Management can coordinate sheets and review calendars while each entity checks its own documents. Keep the dated description used for proposals. Price differences can then be traced to underlying information.

Include vacant and storage-only spaces. They remain part of building assessment despite generating no sales. Actual-use descriptions reduce uncertainty between owner, manager and assessor.

Frequently asked questions about shopping centres

Can the owner automatically insure tenants' stock?

Do not infer this from the policy name. Identify property, parties and interests in documents before telling tenants their stock is protected.

What is needed initially?

Building and space descriptions, ownership-based inventory, supported values and known incidents are starting points. Additional records or inspection may be required; lists differ by product.

Are shop-closure losses included?

Not automatically. Assess interruption and triggering conditions separately. Lost rent and traders' sales are different interests.

Must information change with a new tenant?

Check activity, property and fit-out differences. New use may require reassessment under proposal or existing-contract conditions.
